title: Humor
hookLine: Zen laughter, Ryokan's games, Ikkyu's jokes
tomorrow: why did an old monk turn down the Buddha's offer of an easier life?

cards: A phone goes off in the middle of a silent exam, and the whole room cracks up. Laughter loves the exact moment it isn't supposed to happen. Zen keeps stories like that.
Here's one people tell about Ikkyu, a Japanese Zen monk remembered for his poems and his jokes. As a boy, he broke his teacher's prized teacup.
He heard the teacher coming, hid the pieces behind his back, and asked: why do people have to die? Everything dies when its time comes, the teacher said. Ikkyu held out the pieces.

teach.b: So can something holy be funny? Zen's answer is the joke itself. The boy didn't dodge the teaching; he handed it back, in pieces.
Whatever comes together comes apart. In the Long Discourses, the Buddha's last words to his monks begin there: all conditioned things pass away.
Seeing that clearly loosens the grip, and in Buddhist teaching the grip, craving and clinging, is where suffering starts. What do we grip hardest?
Ourselves: our dignity, our image, the version of us that never drops anything. A good laugh can pry those fingers open. Zen lore keeps stories of laughing monks.

Ryokan, who, in a story people tell, hid so well in a children's game that he was still hiding the next morning. Budai, the laughing monk with the big belly and the sack. Their lightness isn't careless.
It's not holding on. A neighbor tradition says something close.
Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones."
Both see a light heart as good for a person. The honest difference: Proverbs sets that merry heart inside a life lived before God, as part of wisdom.
The Zen joke points somewhere else: at how little there is to cling to, even in yourself.

how: Zen communities keep funny stories of their teachers and tell them as teachings; the Buddha's teaching on impermanence, that all conditioned things pass away, is recited and reflected on in Buddhist practice.

o: in Zen, laughter that loosens our grip on the self
a Zen rule that every lesson ends with a joke

s: in Zen, laughing during practice is always a failure
Zen lore keeps laughing monks: Ikkyu, Ryokan, Budai. lightness can be the practice.
the Buddha's last words, in the Long Discourses, begin with all conditioned things passing away
Ikkyu's joke points at the same teaching.
Proverbs and Zen laugh for exactly the same reason
both see a light heart as good; Proverbs sets it in a life before God, Zen points at loosening the grip on self.

games.q: you're giving a toast at your cousin's party and your notes blow off the table mid-sentence. everyone gasps. what fits today's teaching?
o: laugh, say 'so much for the notes,' and keep going.
stop and apologize until the room is serious again.
keep a straight face; a laugh would cheapen it.
games.why: Ikkyu met a broken cup with a teaching and a grin. things pass, dignity too; holding the moment lightly lets it go on.

practice: Sit as you are and let three things soften: the shoulders, the jaw, the corners of the mouth. If a smile wants to come, let it; if not, that's fine too.
Then rest with the breath, and hold this moment the way you'd hold a teacup you know won't last forever: carefully, and lightly.

wordCard.voice: Humor: in Zen, a laugh that loosens the grip. Ikkyu's broken teacup, handed back as a teaching.

orig.note: Pali: impermanence, what Ikkyu's broken cup points to.

carryVoice: The line for today: lightly, the way Ikkyu held out the pieces of the cup. See you tomorrow.
